meaning: What one job in the robot's learning loop hands to the next job, such as a decoded frame, a simulation step, a training sample or an action. You count units of work per second to compare two machines.

A computer that sits next to the robot instead of in the cloud. You buy it once instead of renting it by the hour, so you compare edge computers on the work they do per unit of energy and on their purchase price.
A small program that we ran in place of a real workload. It loads a machine in a similar way to that workload, but it is not the workload itself.
Units of work per second divided by the watts that a machine draws under load. It tells you how much work the machine does with a fixed amount of energy.
The way you buy an hour of an instance: On-Demand, Spot Instances that AWS can reclaim, or capacity reserved in advance. Each purchase option has its own price.
The AWS location that an instance runs in. Prices differ between Regions.

Spot Instances are spare EC2 capacity that AWS can reclaim. For a batch job on Spot Instances, count only the units that finished, because a unit that is lost when AWS reclaims the instance delivers nothing.
One GPU running for one hour.
A program launched on the GPU. The utilisation figure in nvidia-smi counts the time during which at least one kernel is running, not how much of the GPU the kernel uses.
The time between two commands to the motors. It is 33.3 ms when the arm is driven at 30 Hz, and the deadline of a policy call is counted in control periods.
A set of future actions that one policy call returns. The arm plays them one per control period while the next call runs.
Starting the next policy call while the arm is still playing the current chunk, so the arm does not have to stop and wait.
The time within which half of all calls finish. It describes the typical call.
The time within which ninety-nine calls in a hundred finish. You compare it with the time that a chunk leaves for a call when one late call in a hundred is acceptable.

The resource that a workload runs out of first, while the rest of the machine is partly idle. You price a workload on an instance type built around its bottleneck. For the policy test program on the Jetson core, the bottleneck is memory bandwidth.
EC2 GPU instances whose GPUs also have graphics and video hardware, including RT cores.
EC2 GPU instances built for training. Their GPUs do not have RT cores, and the H100 GPUs in P5 cannot decode AV1.
The GPU units that trace rays. A ray-tracing camera renderer needs them.
The video compression format that LeRobot records in by default. Decoding it needs a hardware decoder that supports AV1, or CPU cores.
A robot physics simulator. Our physics and render test programs ran on two MuJoCo releases, 4.0.1 on the Spark and 3.17.0 on the Jetson.
NVIDIA's inference compiler. NVIDIA reports a median GR00T N1.7 call time on a Jetson Orin of 149.0 ms with TensorRT and 357.9 ms in plain PyTorch.
The built-in monitor on a Jetson. It prints the power drawn on each supply line (rail) of the board, and its VDD_IN rail feeds the whole board.
NVIDIA's command-line tool that reports GPU status, including utilisation and the power of the GPU.
AWS's own Arm processors, offered as EC2 CPU instances.
The interface that MuJoCo's offscreen renderer used for hardware-accelerated drawing without a display. Our render run did not establish how much of each frame the GPU drew.

One call in a hundred is slower than the p99. So if you compare the p99 with the time that a chunk leaves for a call, you accept one late call in a hundred. If you accept none, compare the slowest call instead.
The purchase price of a board divided by the units of work per second that it sustains. It tells you what each unit per second of capacity cost to buy.

The three conditions under which a ratio of two rates describes the two machines: the same unit, the same model and the same software release. For a vendor's figure, the runtime and the power mode must match too.
The ratio of two rates that were each measured on one core. It stands for the ratio of the two machines only for a job that keeps one core busy.
One supply line on a board. tegrastats reports the power of each rail, and on a Jetson the VDD_IN rail feeds the whole board.
The tegrastats rail that feeds the whole Jetson board. Read this rail to get the power of the whole board.
The power setting that a Jetson runs in. NVIDIA took its GR00T N1.7 figures in the MAXN mode, and our Jetson ran in the MAXN_SUPER mode. Record the mode with every figure.
The CPU unit that EC2 lists. On most eight-GPU sizes, two vCPUs are two threads of one physical core. On G7, one vCPU is one physical core.
PyTorch's own compiler. It is one of the three runtimes in NVIDIA's GR00T N1.7 latency table.
A neural-network layer that multiplies its input by a weight matrix, so every output depends on every input. The policy test program is six of them, run on one CPU core.

A LeRobot mode that runs the policy in a background thread of the process that drives the arm. If the arm runs out of actions, a supported robot holds its last commanded position for up to one second by default, and then the run stops with a fault.
